families.t: law, machinery, chemicals, dermatitis, noise, manual handling, fire, slips, maintenance and surveillance
f: Printing businesses must manage both safety and occupational-health duties.
HSE printing guidance covers machinery, fire and explosion, slips and trips, chemicals, dermatitis, noise and manual handling.
Historical printing-sector reports identify manual handling, machinery contact and slips or trips as major accident categories.
Risk assessment should consider the actual printing process, equipment, products and tasks.
Safety-related machine features require planned inspection and maintenance.
Training should reflect the press, converting equipment and intervention tasks used.
Chemical control and machine safeguarding should be coordinated rather than treated as separate systems.
Arrangements should be reviewed after equipment, product, solvent, staffing or work-method changes.
families.g: Printing risk depends on process and press type, machinery and safeguarding, inks and solvents, fire loading, manual handling, maintenance, competence and worker health.

families.t: press standards, cylinders, rollers, nips, limited powered movement, hold-to-run control, guards, interlocks and emergency stops
f: Printing presses manufactured or refurbished since 2005 should comply with the relevant BS EN 1010 machinery standard.
Older presses require practicable safeguards for significant hazards.
Roller and cylinder nips should not be accessible during dangerous movement.
Limited powered movement should use defined hold-to-run controls and restricted displacement or speed.
Guards and interlocks should match the press type and access needed.
Emergency stops should support but not replace prevention of access to dangerous movement.
Safety-related features should be checked at risk-based intervals.
Missing, defeated or ineffective guards should be corrected before normal production continues.
families.g: Press-safeguarding risk depends on press type and age, cylinder and roller movement, access, control mode, guards and interlocks, stopping performance, maintenance and operator competence.

families.s: HSE safe systems for cleaning printing presses
families.t: inch-stop-lock-clean, slow crawl, nip bars, powered rollers, hand turning, multi-person work, cleaning chemicals and isolation
f: HSE specifies press-type safe systems for cleaning sheet-fed, web-fed, gravure and flexographic presses.
Inch-stop-lock-clean is a recognised sequence for many cleaning tasks.
Powered rollers should not be cleaned by uncontrolled access to moving nips.
Slow-crawl cleaning is only suitable where the required nip bars and emergency controls are provided.
Free-running rollers may be hand turned where the task and machine allow it safely.
Multi-person cleaning needs communication and control of unexpected movement.
Cleaning chemicals require COSHH controls in addition to machinery controls.
The cleaning method should be documented, trained, supervised and reviewed when press arrangements change.
families.g: Press-cleaning risk depends on press design, nip access, movement mode and speed, isolation and locking, number of people, cleaning tools and chemicals, supervision and maintenance.

families.t: plate development, ink mixing, conventional and UV inks, IPA damping, heat-set and cold-set inks, manual and automatic cleaning, ventilation and skin control
f: Lithographic control sheets cover film and plate development, ink mixing, printing and press cleaning.
Automatic plate development can reduce skin contact and may require extraction for developer fumes.
Conventional, UV-curable, cold-set and heat-set inks require process-specific controls.
IPA damping and cleaning solvents can create inhalation and skin exposure.
Automated cleaning can reduce direct contact but still requires safe chemical handling and maintenance.
Ventilation and enclosure should minimise vapour and mist exposure.
Gloves, eye protection and skin care should control residual contact.
COSHH assessment should use current safety data and reflect the actual ink, coating and cleaning products.
families.g: Lithographic chemical risk depends on ink and coating system, developers and cleaners, IPA and solvent use, process enclosure, ventilation, task duration, skin contact, PPE and maintenance.

families.t: photopolymer plates, solvent-borne inks, UV-curable inks, mixing, printing, press cleaning, ventilation, fire and dermatitis control
f: Flexographic COSHH sheets cover photopolymer plate making, ink mixing, printing and press cleaning.
Solvent-borne ink mixing and printing require vapour controls.
UV-curable ink mixing and printing require skin and sensitisation controls.
Process enclosure and effective ventilation should reduce airborne exposure.
Containers and transfer systems should minimise spills and evaporation.
Cleaning should use the least hazardous effective method and controlled solvent handling.
Reusable or single-use chemical-resistant gloves should match splash and immersion risks.
Fire precautions should reflect solvent inventory, ventilation and ignition sources.
families.g: Flexographic chemical risk depends on plate and ink chemistry, solvent or UV system, mixing and transfer, press enclosure, ventilation, cleaning, skin contact, fire controls and worker susceptibility.
